answer: A state's uniform credentialing and recredentialing policy must address acute, primary, mental health, substance use disorders, and LTSS providers, as appropriate [1].

No. Under 42 CFR 438.214(c), plans cannot discriminate against providers who either serve high-risk populations or practice in a specialty that "require[s] costly treatment" when deciding whether to include providers in their networks [1].

Managed care plans must also not contract with providers excluded from federal health care programs (42 CFR 438.214(d)) [1]. States can establish additional provider selection requirements (42 CFR 438.214(e)) [1].

No. MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs may not employ or contract with providers excluded from participation in Federal health care programs under either section 1128 or section 1128A of the Act [1].

Under the same section, states must ensure through their contracts that MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs terminate any providers of services or persons terminated (as described in section 1902(kk)(8) of the Social Security Act) from participation under this title, title XVIII, or title XXI from participating as a provider in any network [1].

Initial credentialing for physicians and other health care professionals, including members of physician groups, must include a written application, verification of licensure or certification from primary sources, disciplinary status, eligibility for payment under Medicare, and site visits as appropriate. The application must be signed and dated and include an attestation by the applicant of the correctness and completeness of the application and other information submitted in support of the application [1].

Verification from primary sources must also cover a current valid license to practice, and education and training records, including evidence of graduation from the appropriate professional school and completion of a residency or specialty training, if applicable [4].

Yes. For a newly trained healthcare professional who completed all appropriate training and education within the last 12 months, the MA organization may establish a policy that permits initial credentialing for a period of up to 60 days, if it meets the conditions listed in the source. [1]

Those conditions are:
1. Verifying a current, valid license from primary sources. [1]
2. Verifying malpractice settlements from the last 5 years, through the malpractice carrier or the National Practitioner Data Bank; attestation is not accepted. [1]
3. Having a policy and procedure ensuring the practitioner meets all standard credentialing requirements after 60 days. [1]
4. Ensuring the Credentialing Committee reviews the case and makes the final determination about granting the initial 60-day period. [1]

Health care professionals who are not required to be credentialed include:

- Health care professionals permitted to furnish services only under the direct supervision of another practitioner [1]
- Hospital-based health care professionals who provide services to enrollees incident to hospital services, unless they are separately identified in enrollee literature as available to enrollees [1]
- Students, residents, or fellows [1]

A "primary source" is an organization or entity with legal responsibility for originating a document and ensuring the accuracy of the information it conveys [1]. Primary source verification may be achieved through industry-recognized verification sources, and the nationally recognized accrediting organizations specify which sources they consider appropriate primary sources [1]. If an MA organization uses a primary source identified by one of these accrediting organizations, CMS will consider that source acceptable, and the organization should be able to reference which organization identified it [1, 5].

The National Practitioner Data Bank (NPDB) is not a primary source in the strict sense because it has no legal responsibility for issuing a document, but it is generally considered an appropriate verification source by most private accrediting organizations and by CMS [5].

If an MA organization suspends, terminates, or non-renews a physician's contract, it must give the physician written notice of the reasons, including, if relevant, the standards and profiling data used and the numbers and mix of physicians needed [1]. The physician must be allowed to appeal, and the plan must give written notice of the right to a hearing and the process and timing for requesting one [1]. Adverse participation decisions require written notice and a process for appeal [2].

Under the 1999 final rule preamble, these notice and appeal requirements apply whether or not the action is due to quality deficiencies, unless the physician voluntarily agreed to leave the network [1].

An MA organization must check the OIG sanction list with each new issuance of the list, because it is prohibited from hiring, continuing to employ, or contracting with individuals named on that list [1]. The MA organization should check the OIG website for the listing of excluded providers and entities [1]. The OIG has a limited exception that permits payment for emergency services provided by excluded providers under certain circumstances, see 42 CFR 1001.1901 [1].

Separately, the MA organization must develop and implement policies addressing ongoing monitoring of sanctions, and CMS requires ongoing monitoring of lists of sanctioned practitioners [5]. MA organizations must also monitor sanctions and limitations on licensure on a regular basis between recredentialing cycles [5].

States must revalidate a provider's Medicaid enrollment at least once every five years (42 CFR 455.414) [1]. Ohio requires some providers to revalidate every three years to align with recredentialing [2].
The provider must submit fingerprints within 30 days of the request (42 CFR 455.434). [1]

Under federal law, a managed care plan must terminate the agreement if the state denies the provider's application or if 120 days have passed and the state has not executed the provider agreement (42 CFR 438.602(b)(2)) [1].

Providers in small practices and non-institutional providers such as doulas and community health workers (CHWs) find enrollment and credentialing especially hard mainly because they are newer to the Medicaid program and lack administrative support for these processes [1][2]. Lengthy processes can also cause financial hardship by delaying their ability to bill Medicaid for services delivered [2].

Doulas in particular may lack prior experience enrolling as Medicaid providers, and because they historically worked as independent contractors, they may be unaccustomed to working with health plans and unfamiliar with Medicaid billing practices [4]. More generally, these providers may have less experience and familiarity with these processes than traditional medical providers, and some states require them to take additional steps to enroll or credential [3].

Most Medicare providers and suppliers must revalidate their enrollment every 5 years, while suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) must revalidate every 3 years [1, 4]. CMS may also perform off-cycle revalidations when it deems necessary [1, 2].

Yes. Suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies must revalidate every 3 years, while all other providers and suppliers must revalidate every 5 years [1]. Revalidation is the process of periodically revalidating a Medicare enrollment record through the CMS enrollment application process [1].

The excerpts do not say whether Medicare Advantage plans must ask their physicians for input on credentialing rules. They do say that an MA organization operating a coordinated care plan or network MSA plan must provide for physician participation through reasonable procedures that include written notice of participation rules, including credentialing, before those rules take effect [4]. It must also give written notice of material changes to those rules before the changes take effect, and written notice of adverse participation decisions with a process for appeal [4]. These procedures must apply equally to physicians in subcontracted groups [4].
